data: NASA Langley Research Center / Martin Marietta
Companion orbiter to Viking-1 lander — relay + 50000 surface images at 150-300 m/pixel, the first global Mars map. Operated 1976-1980

The orbital half of NASA's Viking 1 mission — the first US Mars orbiter and one of two near-identical Viking orbiters that returned ~50,000 surface images at 150-300 m/pixel between 1976 and 1980. Launched 1975-08-20 from Cape Canaveral on a Titan IIIE-Centaur, Viking 1 entered Mars orbit 1976-06-19; the orbiter spent a month surveying candidate landing sites before releasing the Viking 1 lander 1976-07-20 to the first successful US Mars landing at Chryse Planitia. The orbiter then continued as a science platform for nearly four more years, building the first global topographic + thermal map of Mars, surveying Phobos + Deimos, and acting as a UHF relay for the lander. Out of attitude-control gas 1980-08-07. Orbit was raised to a high park orbit in 1980 to prevent Mars impact; current status unconfirmed.

Launched 1975-08-20 from Cape Canaveral on a Titan IIIE-Centaur, Viking 1 entered Mars orbit 1976-06-19; the orbiter spent a month surveying candidate landing sites before releasing the Viking 1 lander 1976-07-20 to the first successful US Mars landing at Chryse Planitia. The orbiter then continued as a science platform for nearly four more years, building the first global topographic + thermal map of Mars, surveying Phobos + Deimos, and acting as a UHF relay for the lander. Out of attitude-control gas 1980-08-07. Deliberately raised to a 357 × 33614 km park orbit that's expected to remain stable through ~2024 (decayed ~2025 per Aerospace Corp re-entry forecast).
First spacecraft to encounter Saturn — Jupiter flyby in 1974 then gravity-assist to Saturn in 1979
Only spacecraft to visit all four giant planets
First spacecraft to traverse the asteroid belt
First spacecraft to orbit another planet
Third US lunar orbiter (1967-02-08). Photographed Surveyor 1 sitting on the lunar surface — first photo of a spacecraft on another world

Returned over 50,000 images of Mars's surface and moons over four years. Mapped potential landing sites in advance for both Viking landers. Ended operations in August 1980 when its attitude-control gas was depleted.
